clue: Golf's Masters Tournament has been played every April at a former plant nursery here since 1934.
fact: The winner receives a green jacket that must stay at the club.

clue: Abolitionist John Brown raided the federal armory in this town where two rivers meet, in October 1859.
fact: Robert E. Lee led the Marines who captured Brown.

clue: Napoleon met his final defeat on these fields on June 18, 1815.
fact: A 141-foot artificial hill topped with a lion statue marks the battlefield.

clue: Rome razed this Phoenician city in 146 BC after three wars; its ruins now lie in a capital's suburbs.
fact: Its general Hannibal once crossed the Alps with war elephants.

clue: The spot in the ocean farthest from any land — so remote that the nearest humans are often astronauts overhead.
fact: Space agencies crash old satellites and space stations here.

clue: A painted concrete buoy here marks the southernmost point of the continental U.S., "90 miles to Cuba."
fact: Ernest Hemingway wrote here; descendants of his six-toed cats still live at his house.

clue: The "Wizard" of this village demonstrated a practical incandescent light bulb here in 1879.
fact: Henry Ford later moved the lab to his museum in Michigan.

clue: A Gothic clock tower at the north end of the Houses of Parliament, universally known by the nickname of the great bell inside it.
fact: The clock is fine-tuned by adding or removing old pennies on its pendulum.

clue: An eruption of this glacier-capped volcano in April 2010 sent up an ash cloud that grounded about 100,000 flights across Europe.
fact: Newscasters struggled to pronounce its name.

clue: Confucius was born in 551 BC near this city, and his descendants lived in its family mansion for more than 2,000 years.
fact: The family tree has more than 2 million registered members.

clue: A coffee chain named after a Moby-Dick character opened its first store near this public market in 1971.
fact: The original store has moved once, to a spot a block away.

clue: A woman was acquitted of killing her father and stepmother with a hatchet in this mill city in 1892.
fact: Lizzie Borden's house is now a bed and breakfast.

clue: An island nation's tallest peak, a near-perfect volcanic cone that last erupted in 1707.
fact: The land above the 8th station belongs to a Shinto shrine.

clue: The Pharos lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, stood on an island just off this Mediterranean port.
fact: A medieval fort now sits on the lighthouse's foundations.

clue: The Knights of St. John built this fortified island capital after surviving an Ottoman siege in 1565.
fact: In WWII Britain awarded the whole island the George Cross for enduring relentless bombing.

clue: A 25-hour British bombardment of this star-shaped fort in 1814 inspired the lyrics of the national anthem.
fact: The flag that flew that night is now at the Smithsonian.

clue: Roughly half of the U.S. government's gold reserves sit in a granite bullion vault on this Army post.
fact: Visitors are not allowed inside; only one group tour has ever been given, in 2017.

clue: Roald Amundsen's Norwegian team reached this point on December 14, 1911, beating Robert Falcon Scott by five weeks.
fact: Scott's entire party died on the way back.

clue: The armistice that halted a 1950–53 war was signed at this village inside a demilitarized zone.
fact: No peace treaty has ever been signed.

clue: Billionaires and heads of state gather each January at this Alpine ski town for the World Economic Forum.
fact: It was a tuberculosis sanatorium resort before it was a summit town; it inspired Thomas Mann's 'The Magic Mountain.'

clue: Giant white letters put up on a hillside in 1923 to advertise a real-estate development, originally ending in "LAND."
fact: Each letter is about 45 feet tall.

clue: In a 1976 blind tasting in Paris, wines from this valley beat top French bottles and stunned the wine world.
fact: The event became known as the 'Judgment of Paris.'

clue: Howard Carter found the nearly intact tomb of a boy pharaoh here in November 1922.
fact: Tutankhamun's tomb held more than 5,000 objects.

clue: Tourists rub the bronze breast of a statue beneath 'Juliet's balcony' in this northern Italian city.
fact: Its Roman arena, older than the Colosseum, still stages operas every summer.

clue: Terrorist bombs tore through two nightclubs in this surf town on a Hindu-majority Indonesian island in October 2002.
fact: The attack killed 202 people, including 88 Australians.

clue: Robert E. Lee surrendered his army to Ulysses S. Grant in a private home's parlor here in April 1865.
fact: Wilmer McLean, the home's owner, had moved there to escape the war.

clue: A mountain carving of a Lakota warrior on horseback, begun in 1948 and still unfinished.
fact: When finished, it would be the largest mountain carving in the world.

clue: A harborside performing-arts center with sail-like shells, designed by a Danish architect who quit the project years before it opened in 1973.
fact: Jørn Utzon never returned to see it finished.

clue: Eva Perón addressed huge crowds from the balcony of this pink presidential palace.
fact: Madonna sang "Don't Cry for Me Argentina" from the same balcony in the 1996 film "Evita."

clue: The European Parliament holds its monthly plenary sessions in this Alsatian city on the Rhine, which has switched between France and Germany four times.
fact: Gutenberg worked on his printing press here before moving back to Mainz.

clue: The most famous Mardi Gras in America climaxes on Fat Tuesday in this city.
fact: Throwing beads from parade floats dates back to the late 1800s.

clue: The largest privately owned house in the U.S., a 250-room chateau completed for George Vanderbilt in 1895.
fact: It has 43 bathrooms.

clue: A city built on more than 100 islands in a lagoon, where gondolas glide down a Grand Canal.
fact: There are no cars anywhere in the historic city.

clue: Two cities on opposite banks of the Danube merged with a third in 1873 to form this capital.
fact: Its metro line, opened in 1896, is the oldest in continental Europe.

clue: Helicopters lifted evacuees off a rooftop in this city in April 1975, just before it fell to communist forces.
fact: It was renamed a year later.

clue: The Colonial Revival mansion the King of Rock and Roll bought in 1957, and where he is buried.
fact: It is one of the most-visited private homes in America.

clue: Brigham Young led Mormon pioneers into this valley in July 1847, declaring 'This is the place.'
fact: The city's grid is numbered outward from Temple Square.

clue: The world's tallest freestanding structure from 1975 to 2007, with a glass floor 1,122 feet up.
fact: You can walk around its outside ledge on a tether.

clue: About 1,400 CIA-trained exiles landed here in April 1961 and were defeated within three days.
fact: Cuba later traded the prisoners to the U.S. for $53 million in food and medicine.

clue: Africa's most populous city, the birthplace of Afrobeat pioneer Fela Kuti and home of the 'Nollywood' film industry.
fact: It was the national capital until 1991, when the government moved to Abuja.

clue: Riots after a police raid on a Greenwich Village bar in June 1969 launched the modern gay rights movement.
fact: It became the first national monument dedicated to LGBTQ history in 2016.

clue: A high-school teacher was tried in 1925 for teaching evolution in this small town's courthouse.
fact: William Jennings Bryan died five days after the trial ended.

clue: A vast cobblestone square beside a fortress, home to onion-domed St. Basil's Cathedral and a revolutionary leader's embalmed body.
fact: Its name comes from an old Russian word that meant "beautiful."

clue: The U.S. has leased a naval base on this Caribbean bay since 1903; a military detention camp opened there in 2002.
fact: The U.S. still mails Cuba a rent check of about $4,085 a year, which Cuba refuses to cash.

clue: This city-state was expelled from Malaysia in 1965 and later banned the sale of chewing gum.
fact: Its Changi Airport has a 130-foot indoor waterfall.

clue: The brick statehouse where both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were debated and signed.
fact: The Liberty Bell now hangs in a pavilion across the street.

clue: The first women's rights convention in the U.S. was held here in July 1848.
fact: Elizabeth Cady Stanton modeled its Declaration of Sentiments on the Declaration of Independence.

clue: Longitude 0°: the Prime Meridian runs through an old astronomical observatory in this London borough.
fact: A red ball on the roof drops at 1 p.m. every day for ships to set their clocks.

clue: Most historians believe Christopher Columbus first came ashore in the Americas on this island in October 1492.
fact: The native Lucayans called it Guanahani.

clue: The eastern end of the world's longest railway, about 5,772 miles from the capital.
fact: The trip takes about a week without stops.

clue: Two bicycle makers from Ohio made the first powered, controlled airplane flight on the sand dunes here in December 1903.
answer: Kill Devil Hills (Kitty Hawk), North Carolina
fact: The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet.

clue: A series of 1811–12 earthquakes centered here were so strong they briefly made a major river flow backward.
fact: Church bells reportedly rang as far away as Boston.

clue: Reactor No. 4 exploded here in April 1986, the worst nuclear disaster in history.
fact: The neighboring city of Pripyat was evacuated and remains a ghost town.

clue: Jewish rebels held out on this clifftop fortress above the Dead Sea until the Romans breached it in 73 or 74 AD.
fact: The Roman siege ramp is still there.

clue: France's oldest city, founded by Greek sailors around 600 BC; volunteers marching from here gave the national anthem its name.
fact: The Château d'If prison offshore held the fictional Count of Monte Cristo.

clue: The view from this 14,115-foot summit inspired Katharine Lee Bates to write "America the Beautiful" in 1893.
fact: A car race to its summit has been held since 1916.

clue: A 50,000-year-old impact crater nearly a mile wide in the desert.
fact: Apollo astronauts trained here.

clue: Runners race bulls through the streets here every July during the Festival of San Fermín.
fact: Ernest Hemingway made it famous in "The Sun Also Rises."

clue: A rocky headland at the southern tip of South America, the most feared shipping route before the Panama Canal.
fact: Sailors who rounded it earned the right to wear a gold earring.

clue: Two giant 6th-century Buddha statues carved into cliffs above this valley were blown up by the Taliban in March 2001.
fact: The taller one was about 175 feet.

clue: The oldest institution of higher learning in the U.S., founded in 1636.
fact: It was named for a minister who left it his library and half his estate.

clue: The northern end of a roughly 2,200-mile footpath that starts in Georgia.
fact: About one in four who attempt the full trail finish it.

clue: A tiny bronze statue of a boy relieving himself into a fountain is the mascot of this capital.
fact: He has a wardrobe of more than 1,000 costumes.

clue: A 2015 earthquake toppled the nine-story Dharahara tower and damaged centuries-old temples in this Himalayan capital.
fact: Its valley holds seven UNESCO World Heritage monument zones.

clue: The westernmost point of mainland Europe, a cliff above the Atlantic.
fact: A poet's line there says it's "where the land ends and the sea begins."

clue: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech from these marble steps in August 1963.
fact: The spot where he stood is engraved on the 18th step.

clue: The last major clash of the Indian Wars, in December 1890, on the Pine Ridge Reservation.
fact: Activists occupied the site for 71 days in 1973.

clue: "Mad" King Ludwig II's fairy-tale castle in the Alps, said to have inspired Sleeping Beauty's castle.
fact: Ludwig lived there only 172 days before his mysterious death.

clue: The Titanic was designed and built at a shipyard in this city, where two giant yellow cranes nicknamed Samson and Goliath still tower over the docks.
fact: Locals like to say: 'She was all right when she left here.'

clue: Bob Marley's former home in this capital is now a museum devoted to the reggae legend.
fact: Bullet holes from a 1976 assassination attempt on Marley are still visible there.

clue: A three-day engagement fought July 1–3, 1863, resulting in a major Union victory that marked the turning point of the Civil War — and later a two-minute presidential speech.
fact: The Gettysburg Address was only about 270 words long.

clue: The official end of a 2,000-mile wagon route from Missouri, at a waterfall town on the Willamette.
fact: About 400,000 people traveled the trail.

clue: The first atomic bomb used in war exploded over this city on August 6, 1945; a domed exhibition hall near ground zero survives as a ruin.
fact: The Genbaku Dome was left unrepaired as a memorial.

clue: Giant figures of a hummingbird, monkey and spider were scratched into the desert here around 2,000 years ago.
fact: They are best seen from the air.

clue: A storm in 1850 uncovered a 5,000-year-old Stone Age village on Orkney, complete with stone beds and dressers.
fact: People lived there for about 600 years.

clue: British general Cornwallis surrendered here in October 1781, effectively ending the Revolutionary War.
fact: The British band reportedly played "The World Turned Upside Down."

clue: The largest single-stem tree on Earth by volume, a giant sequoia named for a Civil War general.
answer: General Sherman Tree, Sequoia National Park
fact: It's roughly 2,200 years old.

clue: Thousands of limestone towers rise out of emerald water in this bay in the Gulf of Tonkin; the name means "descending dragon."
fact: There are about 1,600 islands and islets.

clue: Joan of Arc was burned at the stake in this city's marketplace in 1431, aged about 19.
fact: The Church declared her a saint in 1920.

clue: Every August, thousands of people pelt each other with about 120 tons of ripe tomatoes in this small town.
fact: The fight began as a street brawl in 1945.

clue: Twenty-four brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement under a tree here in 1792, founding America's biggest stock exchange.
answer: New York Stock Exchange, Wall Street
fact: The street takes its name from a 17th-century Dutch defensive wall.

clue: Ancestral Puebloans built a 150-room dwelling into a sandstone alcove here around 1200 AD.
fact: Two cowboys searching for stray cattle spotted it in 1888.

clue: The most visited stretch of a defensive barrier thousands of miles long, northwest of a capital; President Nixon walked it in 1972.
fact: Contrary to legend, the wall is not visible to the naked eye from the Moon.

clue: Six Marines raised a U.S. flag on this volcano's summit in February 1945, captured in a Pulitzer-winning photo.
fact: Three of the six were killed later in the battle.

clue: The longest battle of WWI, about 300 days in 1916, was fought around this fortress town under the rallying cry "They shall not pass."
fact: Nine villages destroyed in the fighting were never rebuilt but still have mayors.

clue: The "Mother Church of Country Music," which hosted the Grand Ole Opry radio show from 1943 to 1974.
fact: It was built in 1892 as a tabernacle for revival meetings.

clue: Kids' baseball teams from around the world play for a championship here every August.
fact: Little League was founded here in 1939.

clue: Thousands of vermilion torii gates form tunnels up a sacred mountain at this Shinto shrine.
fact: Each gate is donated by a person or business.

clue: Tens of thousands of stampeders poured into this town during the Klondike Gold Rush of 1896–99.
fact: Jack London came here searching for gold.

clue: A 100-foot bronze statue of the sun god Helios, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, stood at this island harbor until an earthquake toppled it in 226 BC.
fact: It stood for only about 54 years.

clue: A 2.5-mile oval where the winner of a Memorial Day weekend 500-mile race celebrates by drinking milk.
fact: The track was once paved with 3.2 million bricks; a one-yard strip remains at the finish line.

clue: For part of the year, this is the first place in the U.S. to see the sunrise.
fact: It's the highest point on the U.S. Atlantic coast.

clue: A Nabataean city carved into rose-red sandstone cliffs, reached through a narrow gorge called the Siq.
fact: Its Treasury facade appears in "Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade."

clue: Dark and sandy rivers flow side by side for miles without mixing near this Amazon city.
fact: The difference in temperature and speed keeps them apart.

clue: The leaders of the three Allied powers met at this Tudor-style palace in July 1945 to decide the fate of their defeated enemy.
fact: Churchill was voted out of office halfway through the meeting.

clue: The first shots of the Civil War were fired at this island fort in April 1861.
fact: No one was killed in the bombardment itself.

clue: Two childhood friends from Seattle founded a software company in this city in 1975.
fact: Microsoft moved to the Seattle area in 1979.

clue: The walled imperial palace of the Ming and Qing emperors for nearly 500 years, said to hold 9,999 rooms.
fact: Ordinary people were barred from entering for five centuries.

clue: The capital of the Inca Empire, where Spanish colonists built churches on top of Inca stone walls.
fact: Its walls are fitted so tightly that a knife blade can't slip between the stones.

clue: Seven popes ruled the Catholic Church from a giant Gothic palace in this Rhône city in the 1300s instead of from Rome.
fact: Its half-ruined bridge is the subject of a famous French children's song.

clue: The launch pad from which three astronauts lifted off for the first Moon landing on July 16, 1969.
answer: Launch Complex 39A, Kennedy Space Center, Florida
fact: The same pad later launched Space Shuttles and SpaceX rockets.

clue: A 1901 gusher on a salt dome here launched a statewide oil boom.
fact: It sprayed oil 150 feet high for nine days.

clue: Known locally as "the smoke that thunders," this waterfall on the Zambezi was named by David Livingstone for his queen.
fact: Its spray can be seen from more than 20 miles away.

clue: A glacier-fed turquoise lake in the Rockies, framed by Victoria Glacier.
fact: Its color comes from finely ground "rock flour."

clue: Mother Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity in this city in 1950 and is buried there.
fact: It was the capital of British India until 1911.

clue: A suspension bridge painted "International Orange," opened in 1937 across the strait at the mouth of a famous bay.
fact: The color was chosen partly so ships could see it in fog.

clue: Hundreds of thousands of bikers descend on this town every August for a motorcycle rally.
fact: It started in 1938 with nine racers.

clue: The first known cluster of COVID-19 cases was linked to a seafood market in this city in December 2019.
fact: It went into a 76-day lockdown in early 2020.

clue: A mosque built partly over the Atlantic, with a 689-foot minaret — one of the tallest in the world.
fact: Its roof can slide open to the sky.

clue: Frida Kahlo was born, lived and died in a cobalt-blue house in this city's Coyoacán neighborhood.
fact: Leon Trotsky lived there in exile for two years.

clue: Passengers from the Mayflower founded a colony here in December 1620.
fact: The Mayflower actually landed first at Provincetown on the tip of Cape Cod.

clue: Legend says bluesman Robert Johnson sold his soul to the devil at a crossroads in this Delta town.
fact: The crossroads is marked by a sign with three guitars.

clue: The Beatles played nearly 300 shows in this cellar club between 1961 and 1963.
fact: Brian Epstein first saw them here and became their manager.

clue: Heinrich Schliemann dug here in the 1870s, looking for the city from Homer's "Iliad."
fact: Archaeologists have found at least nine cities built on top of each other.

clue: A 1,000-foot cliff often billed as the northernmost point of mainland Europe, where the midnight sun shines from mid-May to late July.
fact: The true northernmost point is a nearby headland you have to hike to.

clue: A seamstress's arrest here in December 1955 sparked a bus boycott that lasted 381 days.
fact: Rosa Parks was 42 when she refused to give up her seat.

clue: In January 1919, a tank burst and sent a 25-foot wave of molasses through this neighborhood, killing 21.
fact: Locals claim the area smelled of molasses on hot days for decades.

clue: The surviving retaining wall of the Second Temple, destroyed by Rome in 70 AD, where visitors tuck written prayers into the cracks.
fact: More than a million notes are cleared out twice a year.

clue: Ancient pilgrims traveled to a mountainside sanctuary here to consult a priestess known as the Oracle.
fact: The Greeks considered it the center of the world.

clue: Watson and Crick announced they had found 'the secret of life' — DNA's double helix — at the Eagle pub in this university town in 1953.
fact: Isaac Newton studied and taught at its Trinity College.

clue: "The Happiest Place on Earth" opened in 1955 on former orange groves.
fact: Walt Disney kept a private apartment above the firehouse on Main Street, U.S.A.

clue: The largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, with a 100-foot earthen mound, across the river from a big Midwestern city.
fact: Around 1100 AD, it may have been larger than London was at the time.

clue: A tidal island topped by a medieval abbey; some of Europe's biggest tides cut it off from the mainland.
fact: Only about 30 people live there.

clue: German and Italian planes bombed this town in April 1937, inspiring one of Pablo Picasso's most famous paintings.
fact: The painting didn't come to Spain until 1981.

clue: A magnitude 7.0 earthquake in January 2010 flattened much of this capital, including its presidential palace.
fact: The quake killed an estimated 100,000 to 300,000 people.

clue: The riverside plantation estate where the first U.S. president lived and died.
fact: George Washington is buried in a tomb on the grounds.

clue: A two-story house with a studio in the basement launched the Supremes, the Temptations and Stevie Wonder.
fact: Berry Gordy started the label with an $800 family loan.

clue: The treaty formally ending World War I was signed in this palace's Hall of Mirrors in June 1919.
fact: The hall has 357 mirrors.

clue: Alan Turing and other codebreakers cracked the German Enigma cipher at this country estate during WWII.
fact: Its work was kept secret until the 1970s.

clue: The Apostle Paul was said to be converted on the road to this city, often called the oldest continuously inhabited capital.
fact: Damascus steel was prized for blades with a watery, rippled pattern.

clue: A surprise attack on a Sunday morning in December 1941 — "a date which will live in infamy" — brought the U.S. into World War II.
fact: The USS Arizona Memorial straddles the sunken battleship, which still leaks drops of oil.

clue: A peanut farmer from this tiny town became the 39th president.
fact: Jimmy Carter lived to 100, the longest-lived president.

clue: A Jewish teenager hid for two years in a secret annex behind a bookcase in this canal house during WWII, and kept a famous diary.
fact: Her father, Otto, was the family's only survivor.

clue: British forces won a colony from France in a 15-minute battle here in 1759; both commanding generals died.
fact: The battlefield is now a city park.

clue: Leo Tolstoy was born, wrote "War and Peace," and is buried on this country estate.
fact: His grave has no cross or headstone.

clue: A concrete arch-gravity dam completed in 1936 in a desert canyon on a state border, holding back the largest reservoir in the U.S.
fact: It holds enough concrete to pave a two-lane highway from San Francisco to New York.

clue: A stone monument near this town marks the geographic center of the contiguous U.S.
fact: It's been the official center since 1918.

clue: Twin-spired Gothic cathedral that took more than 600 years to finish and survived 14 hits by Allied bombs in WWII.
fact: It was the tallest building in the world from 1880 to 1884.

clue: At nearly 12,000 feet, the highest seat of government in the world; commuters ride cable cars over the city.
fact: Its airport, up in neighboring El Alto, sits at about 13,300 feet.

clue: Whitewashed, blue-domed villages cling to the rim of a flooded volcanic caldera on this Aegean island.
fact: A Bronze Age eruption here may have inspired the legend of Atlantis.

clue: A 102-story Art Deco skyscraper completed in 1931 in just 410 days; King Kong climbed it in 1933.
answer: Empire State Building, New York City
fact: It has its own ZIP code: 10118.

clue: Two rivers meet to form a third at a fountain-tipped park in this city.
fact: Fort Pitt once stood here.

clue: Toss a coin over your shoulder into this Baroque fountain and you're supposed to return to its city.
fact: Roughly €1 million in coins are collected each year and given to charity.

clue: The first Winter Olympics were held in this Alpine town below Mont Blanc in 1924.
fact: A U.S. speed skater won the first gold medal.

clue: Two U.S. Black Hawk helicopters were shot down over this city in October 1993.
fact: The battle became the book and film "Black Hawk Down."

clue: North America's tallest peak, at 20,310 feet.
fact: Measured base to summit, it's taller than Everest.

clue: A 1,348-foot earthwork in the shape of a snake winding along a ridge.
fact: Its builders and exact age are still debated.

clue: The Avenue of the Dead links the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon in this ancient city northeast of a modern capital.
fact: The Aztecs found it already abandoned and gave it its name.

clue: Hammurabi and Nebuchadnezzar ruled from this ancient city on the Euphrates.
fact: Its Ishtar Gate was rebuilt in a Berlin museum.

clue: Captured U.S. pilots, including future senator John McCain, were held in a French-built prison that they sarcastically nicknamed after a hotel chain, in this capital.
fact: Its Old Quarter streets were once each named for the single trade practiced there.

clue: The longest suspension bridge in the world when it opened in 1883; P.T. Barnum marched 21 elephants across to prove it was sturdy.
fact: Its chief engineer's wife, Emily Roebling, oversaw construction after he fell ill.

clue: Two young men built their first motorcycle in a 10-by-15-foot backyard shed here in 1903.
fact: The city's breweries once made it the beer capital of the world.

clue: A Roman town buried under volcanic ash when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD.
fact: Plaster casts preserve the shapes of victims where they fell.

clue: Pan Am Flight 103 was brought down by a bomb over this small town in December 1988, killing 270.
fact: Thirty-five of the victims were Syracuse University students.

clue: The "Polar Bear Capital of the World," a Hudson Bay town where bears gather each fall waiting for the ice.
fact: The town has a polar bear "jail" for bears that wander in.

clue: Baseball's Hall of Fame opened in this village in 1939, based on a myth that the game was invented here.
fact: The myth credited Abner Doubleday, who never claimed to have invented baseball.

clue: Wild Bill Hickok was shot dead at a poker table in this gold-rush town in 1876, holding aces and eights.
fact: That hand is still known as the "dead man's hand."

clue: A marble bell tower that began tilting in the 1170s, during construction, because of soft ground.
fact: A decade-long project ending in 2001 reduced the lean by about 17 inches.

clue: The asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago left a crater centered near this coastal village.
fact: The crater is buried and was found by oil geologists.

clue: The world's tallest building from 2004 to 2010, with a 730-ton steel ball hanging inside to steady it against typhoons.
fact: Its New Year's fireworks are launched from the tower itself.

clue: A pharmacist first sold a soda at Jacobs' Pharmacy here in 1886 for five cents a glass.
fact: The original Coca-Cola recipe included coca leaf extract.

clue: Two Stanford grads started an electronics company in a garage on Addison Avenue in 1939.
fact: It's officially designated "the Birthplace of Silicon Valley."

clue: The cube-shaped shrine at the center of Islam's holiest mosque, which pilgrims circle seven times during the Hajj.
fact: Non-Muslims are not permitted to enter the city.

clue: A 13-story palace at about 12,000 feet, winter home of the Dalai Lamas until the 14th fled into exile in 1959.
fact: It has more than 1,000 rooms.

clue: Drug lord Pablo Escobar was shot dead on a rooftop in this Colombian city in December 1993.
fact: Outdoor escalators up its hillside neighborhoods helped transform the city's image.

clue: James Marshall spotted flakes of gold at a sawmill here in January 1848, setting off a rush of 300,000 prospectors.
fact: Neither Marshall nor John Sutter got rich from the discovery.

clue: A 51-day standoff between federal agents and a religious sect ended in a fire here in April 1993.
fact: About 76 people died.

clue: Often called the southernmost city in the world, a port on the Beagle Channel where most Antarctic cruises depart.
fact: Its old prison is now a museum.

clue: The Battle of the Boyne, where William of Orange defeated James II in 1690, was fought about 30 miles north of this capital.
fact: The battle is still marked by parades in Northern Ireland every July.

clue: Electrician Lech Wałęsa led strikes at this shipyard in 1980 that created Solidarity, the first free trade union in the Soviet bloc.
fact: Wałęsa later became Poland's president.

clue: Two brothers opened a hamburger stand here in 1940 that grew into the world's biggest fast-food chain.
fact: Ray Kroc bought out the McDonald brothers in 1961.

clue: Delegates from 44 nations met at a grand mountain resort hotel here in 1944 to create the IMF and the World Bank.
fact: They agreed to peg currencies to the dollar.

clue: Finches and giant tortoises on these volcanic Pacific islands helped shape Charles Darwin's thinking after his 1835 visit.
fact: The islands straddle the equator.

clue: King John sealed the Magna Carta in a riverside meadow here in 1215.
fact: The American Bar Association built the memorial on the site.

clue: Thirty-five nations signed the 1975 Accords on security and human rights at a summit in this Nordic capital.
fact: About two-thirds of Finns take a sauna at least once a week; the city has a public one on its harbor.

clue: John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln here during a comedy on April 14, 1865.
fact: The play was "Our American Cousin."

clue: The first moving assembly line for automobiles began at a plant here in 1913.
fact: It cut Model T build time from 12 hours to about 90 minutes.

clue: Twin skyscrapers linked by a sky bridge, the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004.
fact: Their floor plan is based on an eight-pointed Islamic star.

clue: The Nobel Prize banquet is held every December 10 in this building's hall.
fact: It's the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death.

clue: A 74,000-seat stadium nicknamed 'the Theatre of Dreams' in the world's first industrial city.
fact: The 1958 Munich air disaster killed eight of the club's players.

clue: The deepest lake in the U.S., 1,943 feet, fills the caldera of a collapsed volcano.
fact: No rivers flow into or out of it — it's filled by rain and snow.

clue: The world's oldest annual marathon has started in this small town since 1924.
fact: The race is always run on Patriots' Day.

clue: The most famous playwright in the English language was born in this market town in 1564 and is buried in its church.
fact: The curse on his grave warns against moving his bones.

clue: A sheep farm near this North Island town was turned into the Shire for "The Lord of the Rings" films.
fact: The farm's owner kept the hobbit holes as a tourist attraction.

clue: Massive dry-stone walls — built without mortar — mark this medieval African city, which gave its modern country its name.
fact: A soapstone bird found there appears on the national flag.

clue: The domed hilltop home that a Founding Father designed himself — it's on the back of the nickel.
fact: Thomas Jefferson spent more than 40 years building and remodeling it.

clue: Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and the Big Bopper died in a plane crash here in 1959, "the day the music died."
fact: They'd just played the Surf Ballroom.

clue: The largest religious monument in the world, built as a Hindu temple in the 12th century and pictured on its country's flag.
fact: Unusually for the region, it faces west — the direction associated with death.

clue: One of the world's oldest republics, founded in 301 AD according to tradition, perched on a mountain entirely surrounded by another country.
fact: It has more cars than people.

clue: A lone man stood in front of a column of tanks on the avenue beside this capital's central square in June 1989.
fact: His identity has never been confirmed.

clue: A 630-foot stainless-steel arch completed in 1965 to commemorate westward expansion.
fact: It is exactly as wide at its base as it is tall.

clue: On a dueling ledge here in 1804, the sitting vice president fatally shot a former Treasury secretary.
fact: Alexander Hamilton's son had been killed in a duel at the same spot three years earlier.

clue: A planned capital built from scratch in 41 months and inaugurated in 1960, laid out in the shape of an airplane.
fact: Architect Oscar Niemeyer designed most of its major buildings.

clue: Ludwig van Beethoven was born in 1770 in this Rhine city, which later served as a temporary national capital.
fact: Beethoven wrote the Ninth Symphony while almost completely deaf.

clue: Police opened fire on schoolchildren protesting Afrikaans-language instruction in this township outside South Africa's biggest city in June 1976.
fact: Its Vilakazi Street is the only street in the world where two Nobel Peace laureates lived.

clue: One of the world's most active volcanoes, whose summit crater is said to be home of the fire goddess Pele.
fact: It erupted almost continuously from 1983 to 2018.

clue: A salt dome "island" where a famous red pepper sauce has been made since 1868.
fact: The sauce ages in white oak barrels for up to three years.

clue: Britain handed this territory back at midnight on July 1, 1997, after more than 150 years of rule.
fact: The deal promised "one country, two systems" for 50 years.

clue: Europe's most active volcano, towering over a Mediterranean island.
fact: It has been erupting on and off for at least 500,000 years.

clue: Eleven Israeli athletes were taken hostage and killed at the 1972 Summer Olympics in this city.
fact: Mark Spitz won seven gold medals at the same Games.

clue: In 1947 the Army announced it had recovered a "flying disc" from a ranch near this town — then quickly retracted.
fact: The debris was later explained as a classified balloon program called Project Mogul.

clue: The tallest brick lighthouse in America was moved 2,900 feet inland in 1999 to escape erosion.
fact: It's painted with a black-and-white spiral.

clue: Bolsheviks stormed this green-and-white tsarist palace in October 1917; today it's part of the Hermitage Museum.
fact: The museum keeps about 50 cats to hunt mice.

clue: French kings were crowned in this city's cathedral for centuries, and Germany signed its unconditional surrender here in May 1945.
fact: It is the unofficial capital of the Champagne region.

clue: George Clooney owns a villa on this Y-shaped lake near the Swiss border.
fact: Mussolini was captured near its shores while fleeing in 1945.

clue: A glass pyramid on the lakefront houses the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, opened in 1995.
fact: A local DJ, Alan Freed, is credited with popularizing the term "rock and roll."

clue: The only U.S. state capital that can't be reached by road from the rest of the continent.
fact: A glacier sits just 12 miles from downtown.

clue: Filippo Brunelleschi topped this cathedral with the largest brick dome ever built, finished in 1436.
fact: No one knows exactly how he built it without a supporting frame.

clue: William the Conqueror defeated King Harold here in 1066; the town is named after the fight.
fact: Legend says Harold was killed by an arrow in the eye.

clue: The world's oldest surviving parliament first met in this rift valley in 930 AD; the North American and Eurasian plates are pulling apart here.
fact: Snorkelers can touch both continents at once in a fissure called Silfra.

clue: A golden spike driven here in May 1869 completed the first transcontinental railroad.
fact: The actual golden spike is now at Stanford University.

clue: A bomb thrown at a labor rally here in May 1886 is commemorated around the world on May Day.
fact: Four men were hanged for the bombing; three others were later pardoned.

clue: Fidel Castro's rebels rolled into this capital in January 1959; 1950s American cars still cruise its seaside Malecón.
fact: The city was founded by the Spanish in 1519.

clue: Francisco Pizarro founded this 'City of Kings' on the Pacific coast in 1535; it is now its country's capital.
fact: It gets almost no rain, yet sits under a gray sea fog most of the year.

clue: Protesters camped for months in this capital's Maidan square in 2014, and invading troops were turned back from its outskirts in 2022.
fact: Its metro's Arsenalna station is one of the deepest in the world.

clue: The first permanent English settlement in North America, founded in 1607 on a marshy river island.
fact: Captain John Smith later wrote that Pocahontas saved his life here.

clue: The tallest peak in the contiguous U.S., 14,505 feet.
fact: The John Muir Trail ends at its summit.

clue: A Maya city whose step pyramid casts a serpent-shaped shadow down its staircase at the spring and fall equinoxes.
fact: Clapping at the pyramid's base produces an echo like a bird's chirp.

clue: Iraq invaded this oil-rich emirate in August 1990, prompting the first Gulf War.
fact: Retreating troops set more than 600 oil wells on fire.

clue: Commandos flew about 2,500 miles to free hostages from a hijacked airliner at this airport in July 1976.
fact: The only commando killed was Yoni Netanyahu, brother of a future prime minister.

clue: The largest shopping mall in the U.S., opened in 1992 with an indoor theme park at its center.
fact: You could fit seven Yankee Stadiums inside it.

clue: Tens of thousands of shareholders flock here every spring for Warren Buffett's annual meeting, dubbed 'Woodstock for Capitalists.'
fact: The Reuben sandwich is said to have been invented at a hotel here.

clue: A 1,300-foot container ship wedged sideways here in March 2021, blocking one of the world's busiest waterways for six days.
fact: Roughly 12% of global trade passes through the canal.

clue: The holiest shrine of Sikhism, a gold-plated temple set in a sacred pool; its free kitchen serves around 100,000 meals a day.
fact: Anyone of any faith can eat there.

clue: Protestant nobles threw two Catholic officials out of a castle window here in 1618; the officials survived, but a 30-year war followed.
fact: They reportedly landed on a pile of manure.

clue: Defenders including Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie were killed at a Spanish mission here in March 1836.
fact: Its fall became the rallying cry at the Battle of San Jacinto six weeks later.

clue: 146 garment workers, mostly young immigrant women, died in a factory fire near Washington Square in 1911.
answer: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory, New York City
fact: Locked exit doors led to sweeping new fire-safety laws.

clue: More than 330,000 Allied soldiers were evacuated from the beaches here in 1940, many aboard fishing boats and pleasure yachts.
fact: Churchill called it "a miracle of deliverance."

clue: Pilgrims walking the Camino have ended their journey at this city's cathedral, said to hold the remains of the apostle James.
fact: Pilgrims who walk the last 100 km receive a certificate.

clue: Allied bombers created a firestorm in this baroque city in February 1945; Kurt Vonnegut survived it as a prisoner in an underground meat locker.
fact: The experience became his novel "Slaughterhouse-Five."

clue: The deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history, a 1900 hurricane, killed at least 6,000 people on this barrier island.
fact: The city raised its entire grade by up to 17 feet afterward.

clue: The bloodiest single day in American history: about 23,000 casualties along a creek on September 17, 1862.
fact: The Union victory gave Lincoln the opening to issue the Emancipation Proclamation.

clue: A wrought-iron lattice tower built as the entrance arch to the 1889 World's Fair — and denounced by leading artists of the day as "useless and monstrous."
fact: It grows about 6 inches taller in summer as the iron expands.

clue: The deepest known point in any ocean, about 36,000 feet down; James Cameron reached it solo in 2012.
fact: Mount Everest would fit inside with more than a mile to spare.

clue: The America's Cup has been raced on the harbor of this 'City of Sails,' its country's largest city.
fact: It is built on a field of about 50 volcanoes.

clue: The worst commercial nuclear accident in U.S. history, a partial meltdown in March 1979.
fact: The plant's undamaged reactor kept running until 2019.

clue: In 1921 a white mob destroyed the prosperous Black neighborhood here known as "Black Wall Street."
fact: The massacre was largely left out of history books for decades.

clue: A fortress on an extinct volcano above a capital city, where a cannon has fired at 1 p.m. every day since 1861.
fact: The gun let ships in the harbor check their clocks.

clue: A February 2011 earthquake killed 185 people in this city and toppled the spire of its Anglican cathedral.
fact: A temporary "cardboard cathedral" was built afterward.

clue: An oasis city on the caravan routes whose queen, Zenobia, rebelled against Rome; ISIS blew up its Temple of Bel in 2015.
fact: Its ruins include a colonnade more than half a mile long.

clue: A 605-foot flying-saucer-topped tower built for the 1962 World's Fair.
fact: It was built to withstand winds of 200 mph.

clue: The oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the continental U.S., founded by Spain in 1565.
fact: It was founded 42 years before Jamestown.

clue: A rocky hilltop citadel crowned by a marble temple to the goddess Athena, completed in 438 BC.
fact: The Parthenon was used as a gunpowder store and blown up during a siege in 1687.

clue: A gas leak at a pesticide plant here in December 1984 was the world's worst industrial disaster.
fact: At least 3,800 people died almost immediately.

clue: Visitors lie on their backs and lean over a castle parapet here to kiss a stone said to grant the "gift of the gab."
fact: Queen Elizabeth I is said to have coined the word "blarney" out of frustration with the castle's lord.

clue: "One if by land, two if by sea" — two lanterns hung in this church steeple in April 1775 signaled the British were coming by boat.
fact: It is Boston's oldest standing church building, built in 1723.

clue: A rifle heiress kept building this rambling mansion nonstop for 38 years, with stairs leading into ceilings.
fact: It has about 160 rooms.

clue: Nelson Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years in prison on this island.
fact: Former prisoners now lead the tours.

clue: U.S. Marines helped a crowd pull down a giant statue of Saddam Hussein in this capital's central square in April 2003.
fact: The Tigris River runs through the city.

clue: Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at this seaside palace in February 1945 to plan postwar Europe.
fact: FDR died two months later.

clue: The only point in the U.S. where four states meet.
fact: The monument sits on Navajo Nation and Ute Mountain Ute land.

clue: A temporary city of about 70,000 rises each summer and ends by burning a giant wooden effigy.
fact: Organizers insist attendees "leave no trace."

clue: The world's largest beer festival has been held on this meadow since a royal wedding in 1810.
fact: About 7 million liters of beer are served each year.

clue: Crowds clung to a U.S. military plane taking off from this capital's airport during the chaotic evacuation of August 2021.
fact: More than 120,000 people were airlifted out in about two weeks.

clue: The oldest tennis tournament in the world has been played on grass at a club in this suburb since 1877.
fact: Players must wear almost entirely white.

clue: The NFL's oldest continuously used stadium, home of a team owned by its fans.
fact: Players celebrate touchdowns by jumping into the stands.

clue: Lewis and Clark's expedition spent the winter of 1805–06 at a fort they built near the Pacific here.
fact: It rained all but 12 days of their stay.

clue: A 2012 music video that satirized this wealthy district became the first YouTube video to reach a billion views.
fact: The district's name means "south of the river."

clue: A volcanic island between Java and Sumatra whose 1883 eruption was heard nearly 3,000 miles away — the loudest sound in recorded history.
fact: A new island, "Child of Krakatoa," rose from the sea in 1927.

clue: Lions and giraffes roam a national park with a skyline behind it on the edge of this capital; Karen Blixen's 'Out of Africa' farm is in its suburbs.
fact: The UN Environment Programme is headquartered here.

clue: Four presidents, each face about 60 feet tall, were carved into Black Hills granite between 1927 and 1941.
fact: Sculptor Gutzon Borglum died months before it was finished; his son Lincoln completed the work.

clue: A tanker ran aground here in March 1989, spilling about 11 million gallons of crude oil.
fact: It was the largest U.S. oil spill until 2010.

clue: The world's tallest building since 2010, rising 2,717 feet from the desert on the Persian Gulf.
fact: You can watch the sunset from the base, ride up, and watch it again.

clue: Australian and New Zealand troops landed at this cove on April 25, 1915, in a failed campaign to seize the Dardanelles.
fact: April 25 is now a national day of remembrance in both countries.

clue: Towering white chalk cliffs at this port face the narrowest point of a busy channel, just 21 miles from the continent.
fact: On a clear day you can see the far shore.

clue: A granite dome that looks sliced in half, rising nearly 5,000 feet above a famous glacier-carved valley.
fact: Hikers climb the last 400 feet using steel cables.

clue: A 47-day Union siege of this river-bluff city ended on July 4, 1863, splitting the Confederacy in two.
fact: The city didn't officially celebrate July 4th again for decades.

clue: A limestone promontory at the mouth of the Mediterranean, held by the same foreign power since 1713 and home to Europe's only wild monkeys.
fact: Legend says Britain will lose the Rock if the monkeys leave.

clue: Italy's fashion capital, home to the La Scala opera house and a Gothic cathedral with 135 spires.
fact: It co-hosted the 2026 Winter Olympics.

clue: A subtropical Black Sea resort hosted the most expensive Winter Olympics ever, in 2014.

clue: The Flamingo, opened by mobster Bugsy Siegel in 1946, kicked off the casino-resort boom on this desert boulevard.

clue: A town that claims to be the geographic center of North America.

clue: The largest Nazi death camp, liberated by Soviet troops on January 27, 1945.
fact: That date is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

clue: U.S. Navy SEALs killed Osama bin Laden in a walled compound in this garrison city in May 2011.
fact: The compound was demolished in 2012.

clue: Goose-stepping troops and missile launchers parade through this square in a hermit kingdom's capital.
fact: The unfinished 105-story Ryugyong Hotel looms over the city.

clue: A copper gift from France, dedicated in 1886, holding a torch aloft at the entrance to a great harbor.
answer: Statue of Liberty, New York Harbor

clue: The Pony Express began carrying mail from this river town to California in April 1860.
fact: It lasted only 18 months before the telegraph replaced it.

clue: A basalt arch built on the waterfront to welcome King George V; the last British troops left the country through it in 1948.
fact: It faces the Taj Mahal Palace hotel across the plaza.

clue: Queen Elizabeth II died at her Highland country estate here in September 2022.
fact: Prince Albert bought the estate for Queen Victoria in 1852.

clue: Hundreds of thousands of protesters filled this city's central square in 2011, forcing out a president who had ruled for 30 years.
fact: "Tahrir" means "liberation."

clue: A volcano blew out its entire north face on May 18, 1980, killing 57 people.
fact: The eruption took about 1,300 feet off its height.

clue: The oldest state capital in the U.S., where an adobe governor's palace has stood since 1610.
fact: At 7,199 feet, it's also the highest state capital.

clue: A tsunami in March 2011 knocked out cooling at this nuclear plant, leading to three reactor meltdowns.
fact: The quake that caused the tsunami moved Japan's main island about 8 feet east.

clue: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 at this physics laboratory, now home to the Large Hadron Collider.
fact: The first website is still online.

clue: The coldest national capital on Earth, where about half of its country's people live.
fact: A 130-foot steel statue of Genghis Khan stands outside the city.

clue: National Guardsmen killed four students during an antiwar protest on this campus in May 1970.
fact: A photo of a girl kneeling over a slain student won a Pulitzer Prize.

clue: "If you build it, he will come" — a baseball diamond carved from a cornfield here starred in a 1989 film.
fact: MLB played a real game there in 2021.

clue: A 98-foot Art Deco statue with outstretched arms, completed in 1931 atop Corcovado mountain.
answer: Christ the Redeemer, Rio de Janeiro
fact: It's struck by lightning several times a year.

clue: At the 1976 Summer Olympics here, 14-year-old Nadia Comăneci scored gymnastics' first perfect 10.

clue: A famous massacre scene in the 1925 silent film "Battleship Potemkin" was shot on these giant stairs above a Black Sea port.

clue: A truck bomb destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building here on April 19, 1995, killing 168.
fact: The memorial has 168 empty chairs, smaller ones for the 19 children killed.

clue: A wind gust of 231 mph — the fastest ever recorded by a human observer — was measured atop this peak in 1934.
fact: It held the world record for 62 years.

clue: A Gothic cathedral whose spire collapsed in a fire in April 2019; it reopened in December 2024.
fact: Its bells were blessed and rung again for the reopening.

clue: Marie Curie, the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences, was born in 1867 in this capital.
fact: Her notebooks are still too radioactive to handle without protection.

clue: Colonial-era banks line a riverfront promenade facing a skyline of futuristic towers across the Huangpu River.
fact: The city's port is the busiest container port in the world.

clue: Colonists disguised as Mohawk warriors dumped 342 chests of tea into the harbor here in December 1773.
fact: The tea was worth about $1.7 million in today's money.

clue: Two Middle Eastern leaders reached a historic peace framework after 13 days of talks at the presidential retreat here in 1978.
fact: FDR originally called it "Shangri-La."

clue: Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias sailed around this rocky headland in 1488.
fact: Contrary to popular belief, it's not the southernmost point of Africa.

clue: An earthquake, tsunami and fire destroyed most of this capital on All Saints' Day, 1755.
fact: It inspired Voltaire's satire "Candide."

clue: The oldest university in the English-speaking world, where teaching had begun by 1096.
fact: J.R.R. Tolkien and C.S. Lewis both taught there.

clue: The "Great American Race" opens the NASCAR season at a 2.5-mile superspeedway here.
fact: Early races were run on the hard-packed sand of the beach itself.

clue: Henry David Thoreau lived in a one-room cabin by this pond from 1845 to 1847.
fact: The cabin cost him $28.12 to build.

clue: Ships are raised about 54 feet in two steps at these locks near the Pacific end of a canal the U.S. finished in 1914.

clue: Top Nazi leaders were tried for war crimes in Courtroom 600 here in 1945–46.
fact: The courtroom stayed in use for regular trials until 2020.

clue: A small bronze statue of a fairy-tale character, unveiled in 1913, sits on a rock at the edge of this capital's harbor.
fact: She has been beheaded by vandals twice.

clue: A boxer trains by sprinting up the 72 steps of this museum in a 1976 film.
fact: A bronze statue of Rocky stands near the base.

clue: Giant freighters are lifted 21 feet between Lake Superior and Lake Huron at locks here.
fact: Michigan's oldest city, founded in 1668.

clue: Antoni Gaudí's towering basilica, under construction since 1882.
fact: Gaudí is buried in its crypt.

clue: The walled old town of this Adriatic city played King's Landing in "Game of Thrones."
fact: Its city walls run for about 1.2 miles.

clue: Most snorkeling and diving trips to the Great Barrier Reef leave from this tropical Queensland city.
fact: The reef is the largest structure built by living things.

clue: The U.S. Military Academy has trained Army officers on a bluff above the Hudson here since 1802.
fact: Benedict Arnold tried to hand the fort here to the British in 1780.

clue: An offshore drilling rig exploded here in April 2010, causing the largest marine oil spill in history.
answer: Deepwater Horizon site, Gulf of Mexico
fact: The well spewed oil for 87 days.

clue: The ancient Olympic Games were held here starting in 776 BC; the modern Olympic flame is still lit here using a mirror and the sun.
fact: Winners received only an olive wreath.

clue: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in 1756 in this city, which later became the setting for "The Sound of Music."
fact: Mozart wrote his first symphony when he was eight.

clue: The Giralda, a 12th-century minaret turned cathedral bell tower, rises over this Andalusian city, the setting of Bizet's opera 'Carmen.'
fact: Its cathedral is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world.

clue: A geyser in the world's first national park that erupts roughly every 90 minutes.
fact: Its eruptions shoot 100 to 180 feet into the air.

clue: The first atomic bomb was detonated in the desert here at 5:29 a.m. on July 16, 1945.
fact: The blast fused the desert sand into a green glass now called trinitite.

clue: A deep, 23-mile-long lake where sightings of a long-necked monster were reported starting in 1933.
fact: The loch holds more fresh water than all the lakes of England and Wales combined.

clue: A monument here marks the equator — although GPS shows the true line about 800 feet away.
fact: The country is named for the equator.

clue: A Buddhist monastery clinging to a cliff 3,000 feet above a valley, where a guru is said to have flown in on a tigress.
fact: Visitors must hike about two hours to reach it.

clue: Legend blames Mrs. O'Leary's cow for starting a fire that burned more than three square miles of this city in October 1871.
fact: The fire department's training academy now stands on the site of the O'Leary barn.

clue: Four college freshmen started a sit-in at a Woolworth's lunch counter here in February 1960.
fact: A section of the counter is now in the Smithsonian.

clue: The bloodiest of the five Allied landing beaches on June 6, 1944.
fact: The American cemetery on the bluff above holds more than 9,000 graves.

clue: Poppies grow in Flanders fields around this Belgian town, where buglers have sounded the Last Post every evening at the Menin Gate since 1928.
fact: German troops first used chlorine gas here in 1915.

clue: A fortified wine takes its name from this riverside city, where barrels once came down the Douro River on flat-bottomed boats.
fact: J.K. Rowling taught English here while writing early Harry Potter chapters.

clue: The Pro Football Hall of Fame sits in this city, where the NFL was founded in 1920.
fact: The league was founded in a car dealership showroom.

clue: Booker T. Washington founded an institute here in 1881; famous Black WWII pilots trained nearby.
fact: George Washington Carver taught agriculture here for 47 years.

clue: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated near the Latin Bridge in this city in June 1914, setting off World War I.
fact: The driver made a wrong turn that put the car right in front of the gunman.

clue: The Old Course here is known as the "home of golf"; the game has been played on these links since the 1400s.
fact: Its course is closed on Sundays so townspeople can walk it.

clue: An underwater volcano here erupted in January 2022 in the largest explosion ever recorded by modern instruments.
fact: The plume reached the mesosphere, about 35 miles up.

clue: Sentinels have guarded the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier here around the clock since 1937.
fact: The cemetery was established on Robert E. Lee's former estate.

clue: An English colony vanished from this island in the 1580s, leaving only "CROATOAN" carved into a post.
fact: Virginia Dare, the first English child born in the Americas, was among the missing.

clue: A Formula One grand prix has raced through the streets and harbor of this tiny principality since 1929.
fact: Monaco's own citizens are banned from gambling in its casino.

clue: Hundreds of hot-air balloons float at dawn over "fairy chimney" rock spires around this Anatolian town.
fact: Early Christians carved churches and whole underground cities into the soft rock.

clue: British officials and Māori chiefs signed a country's founding treaty here in February 1840.
fact: Its English and Māori versions say different things.

clue: Nineteen people were hanged for witchcraft after trials in this port town in 1692.
fact: A 20th victim, Giles Corey, was pressed to death with heavy stones.

clue: In the first major battle of the Civil War, July 1861, a Confederate general here earned the nickname "Stonewall."
fact: Washington picnickers came out to watch the battle.

clue: A Norman fortress on the Thames that guards the Crown Jewels — legend says the kingdom will fall if its ravens leave.
fact: Two of Henry VIII's wives were beheaded on its grounds.

clue: The hill town that gave its name to the painter of "The Last Supper," born nearby in 1452.
fact: "Da Vinci" just means "from Vinci."

clue: Students seized the U.S. embassy in this capital in November 1979 and held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days.
fact: The hostages were released minutes after Reagan's inauguration.

clue: The first U.S. national monument, a volcanic tower that starred in "Close Encounters of the Third Kind."
fact: Climbers are asked to voluntarily avoid it in June out of respect for tribal ceremonies.

clue: A freighter sank in a November 1975 storm here with all 29 crew — later the subject of a Gordon Lightfoot song.
fact: The ship's bell was recovered in 1995.

clue: The Church of the Nativity, one of the oldest working churches in the world, marks the traditional birthplace of Jesus in this town.
fact: You enter through the "Door of Humility," just 4 feet tall.

clue: A huge market square where snake charmers, storytellers and food stalls take over each night.
fact: UNESCO created a list for "intangible" heritage partly because of this square.

clue: One of the oldest working Christian monasteries, built at the foot of the mountain where Moses is said to have received the Ten Commandments.
fact: It has one of the world's oldest continuously operating libraries.

clue: A twin-spired racetrack that has hosted "the most exciting two minutes in sports" every May since 1875.
fact: The winner is draped in a blanket of more than 400 red roses.

clue: "Oh, the humanity!" — a German airship burst into flames while docking here in May 1937.
fact: Amazingly, 62 of the 97 people aboard survived.

clue: A neoclassical gate that stood stranded in no-man's-land for 28 years until the wall beside it fell in November 1989.
fact: The chariot on top was once carried off to Paris as war loot.

clue: The world's largest power station by capacity, a dam on the Yangtze that displaced more than a million people.
fact: Its reservoir is about 400 miles long.

clue: Three shepherd children reported visions of the Virgin Mary here in 1917; tens of thousands later witnessed a "miracle of the sun."
fact: Two of the children were declared saints in 2017.

clue: A team of U.S. college players beat the Soviet hockey team here in the 1980 "Miracle on Ice."
fact: The village has hosted the Winter Olympics twice.

clue: A mechanical shark nicknamed "Bruce" kept breaking down during filming of a 1975 blockbuster on this island.
fact: The movie's fictional town was called Amity.

clue: A chain of about 275 waterfalls on a border river, whose biggest plunge is called the Devil's Throat.
fact: The falls stretch almost 2 miles.

clue: A messenger supposedly ran about 25 miles from this plain to deliver news of a victory over Persia in 490 BC — then died.
fact: The modern race distance of 26.2 miles was set at the 1908 London Olympics.

clue: A country's Gothic Revival parliament buildings stand on a bluff above a canal that becomes a nearly five-mile skating rink each winter.
fact: The Peace Tower's carillon has 53 bells.

clue: A company town built by a chocolate maker, where streetlights are shaped like foil-wrapped candies.
fact: Milton Hershey built homes, schools and a trolley for his workers.

clue: The southernmost point of all 50 states, on the Big Island.
fact: Polynesian voyagers may have first landed in Hawaii here.

clue: A castle high on a rocky bluff, marketed to tourists as the home of Dracula.
fact: Bram Stoker never visited Romania.

clue: The Romans built a temple and bathhouse around the hot springs in this city.
fact: Jane Austen lived there and set two novels in the city.

clue: Cliff divers plunge more than 100 feet into a narrow ocean cove at this Pacific resort city.
fact: Divers time their jump to land as an incoming wave deepens the water.

clue: A PE instructor at a YMCA training school here invented basketball in 1891 using peach baskets.
fact: James Naismith's original game had 13 rules.

clue: One of ten camps where Japanese Americans were incarcerated during World War II, in the Owens Valley.
fact: About 11,000 people were held there.

clue: The largest church in the world by interior space, crowned by a dome designed by Michelangelo, in the world's smallest country.
fact: It was built over the traditional burial site of the apostle Peter.

clue: The world's largest salt flat, which becomes a giant mirror after rain.
fact: It holds a large share of the world's lithium.

clue: Horatio Nelson's fleet defeated a combined enemy fleet off this cape in 1805; Nelson was killed in the battle.
fact: His body was brought home preserved in a cask of brandy.

clue: A three-day music festival on Max Yasgur's dairy farm drew around 400,000 people in August 1969.
fact: The festival was named for a town about 40 miles away.

clue: The northernmost city in the U.S., where the sun doesn't set for about 80 days each summer.
fact: It was known as Barrow until 2016.

clue: The world's busiest pedestrian scramble, beside a statue of a loyal Akita dog named Hachikō.
fact: Up to 3,000 people can cross at a single change of the lights.

clue: The bloodiest battle in history, fought street by street from 1942 to 1943, turned the tide against Germany in the East.
fact: A statue called "The Motherland Calls" towers over the city.

clue: France's most famous wine region is named for this port city on the Garonne.
fact: Its Water Mirror is the world's largest reflecting pool.

clue: In 1901 a 63-year-old schoolteacher became the first person to survive a trip over these falls — in a barrel.
fact: Annie Edson Taylor made the trip on her birthday, hoping to get rich.

clue: Frank Lloyd Wright's 1935 house cantilevered right over a waterfall on Bear Run.
fact: The owners expected a view of the falls; Wright put the house on top of them.

clue: The monarch's official London residence, where the Changing of the Guard draws crowds and the royal family waves from the balcony.
fact: It has 775 rooms, including 78 bathrooms.

clue: The Blue Nile and White Nile meet to form one river at this capital.
fact: The Blue Nile supplies most of the Nile's water.

clue: The first pope from the Americas was born in this capital in 1936 to Italian immigrants.
fact: Pope Francis died on Easter Monday 2025.

clue: "Don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes" — a June 1775 battle named for one hill but fought mostly on another.
fact: Most of the fighting was on Breed's Hill.

clue: A Ku Klux Klan bombing at a church here killed four girls in September 1963.
fact: The last conviction in the case came in 2002.

clue: Africa's tallest peak, a snow-capped volcano rising alone from the plains near the equator.
fact: It can be climbed without ropes or technical gear.

clue: A munitions ship exploded in this harbor in 1917, the largest human-made explosion before the atomic bomb.
fact: The city still sends Boston a Christmas tree every year to thank it for its help.

clue: Allied bombers destroyed an ancient hilltop abbey here in February 1944, during one of WWII's longest battles.
fact: St. Benedict founded the abbey around 529 AD.

clue: "We've had a problem" — the flight controllers who brought Apollo 13 home worked in a room here.
fact: The Mission Control room used for Apollo was restored in 2019.

clue: The only official royal palace on U.S. soil, home to the last two monarchs of an island kingdom.
fact: It had electric lights before the White House.

clue: A Riviera resort whose film festival awards the Palme d'Or every May.
fact: The festival was first planned for 1939 but canceled when war broke out.

clue: A "doomsday" vault dug into an Arctic mountain stores over a million seed samples from around the world.
fact: Its first withdrawal was in 2015, by researchers from Syria.

clue: Bonnie Prince Charlie's Jacobite army was crushed in under an hour on this moor in April 1746.
fact: Clan stones mark the mass graves.

clue: Twin reflecting pools mark where two 110-story towers stood until September 11, 2001.
answer: World Trade Center, New York City
fact: One World Trade Center is 1,776 feet tall, a nod to 1776.

clue: Land-speed records have been set on this glistening dry lakebed since 1914.
fact: The salt is so flat you can see the curvature of the Earth.

clue: The only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing, built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC.
fact: It was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years.

clue: European powers redrew the map of the continent at a congress in this capital in 1814–15.
fact: Its many balls led one diplomat to say "the Congress dances, but it does not progress."

clue: Goethe was born in this German financial capital, whose skyscraper skyline is nicknamed 'Mainhattan.'
fact: It is home to Germany's busiest airport.

clue: Every February 2, a famous groundhog forecasts the weather at Gobbler's Knob in this town.
fact: The 1993 movie was actually filmed in Woodstock, Illinois.

clue: The U.S. Naval Academy has trained midshipmen in this state capital since 1845.
fact: John Paul Jones is buried in its chapel crypt.

clue: A pyramid-shaped Alpine peak on a border between two countries; four climbers died descending after its first ascent in 1865.
fact: It inspired the Toblerone logo.

clue: The oldest and largest occupied castle in the world, where Prince Harry and Meghan Markle married in St George's Chapel in 2018.
fact: Queen Elizabeth II is buried in the same chapel.

clue: A mountain pass used by invaders for thousands of years and by the British Raj as a frontier post.
fact: A railway through it has 34 tunnels.

clue: A rocky island federal prison from 1934 to 1963 whose inmates included Al Capone.
fact: Three men escaped on a homemade raft in 1962 and were never found.

clue: An island in the straits between two Great Lakes where cars have been banned since 1898.
fact: Getting around is by horse, bicycle or foot.

clue: An amphitheater opened in 80 AD that held around 50,000 spectators for gladiator fights and animal hunts.
fact: Its arena floor hid a two-level maze of tunnels and animal cages.

clue: A snowcapped volcano traditionally named as the landing place of Noah's Ark.
fact: It's the national symbol of neighboring Armenia.

clue: After a dictator fled in 1986, about 3,000 pairs of his wife's shoes were found in the presidential palace in this capital.
fact: A shoe museum in the city later displayed some of them.

clue: A 52-foot freestanding sandstone arch that appears on its state's license plates.
fact: The park it's in has more than 2,000 natural arches.

clue: A 1777 American victory here convinced France to enter the Revolutionary War.
fact: A monument honors Benedict Arnold's wounded leg but not his name.

clue: A prehistoric ring of standing stones on Salisbury Plain, aligned with the midsummer sunrise.
fact: Some of its "bluestones" were hauled about 150 miles from Wales.

clue: Divers rescued 12 boys from a youth soccer team and their coach from this flooded cave in July 2018.
fact: A former Thai Navy SEAL died during the rescue.

clue: Mary and Louis Leakey found some of the earliest human ancestors and stone tools in this ravine near the Serengeti.
fact: The gorge is named after a wild sisal plant.

clue: The Earp brothers and Doc Holliday fought the Clantons and McLaurys in a 30-second gunfight here in October 1881.
fact: The fight actually happened in a vacant lot near the O.K. Corral, not in it.

clue: A sanitarium here gave rise to corn flakes in 1894, earning it the nickname "Cereal City."
fact: The Kellogg brothers fell out over whether to add sugar.

clue: Sheer sea cliffs rising about 700 feet above the Atlantic; they played the Cliffs of Insanity in "The Princess Bride."
fact: Puffins nest on the cliff ledges in summer.

clue: Martin Luther is said to have nailed his Ninety-five Theses to a church door in this town in 1517.
fact: The original wooden door burned in 1760.

clue: Rowboats slip through a tiny opening into the glowing Blue Grotto on this island in the Bay of Naples.
fact: Emperor Tiberius ruled Rome from a villa here for about a decade.

clue: The Continental Army spent the brutal winter of 1777–78 camped here, drilled into shape by a Prussian officer.
fact: About 2,000 soldiers died there, mostly from disease.

clue: Hundreds of thousands of bats spiral out of this cave's mouth at dusk each summer.
fact: Its "Big Room" covers about 8 acres.

clue: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first stood on this summit on May 29, 1953.
fact: The rock at the top is marine limestone — it was once the sea floor.

clue: Lionel Messi finally lifted the World Cup here in December 2022 after a penalty shootout against France.
fact: Qatar built the stadium for the tournament.

clue: A dirt road lined with giant baobab trees, some around 800 years old.
fact: The trees are what's left of a vanished forest.

clue: Visitors can hop across the very beginning of North America's most famous river on stepping stones at this lake.
fact: It takes about 90 days for a drop of water to travel from here to the Gulf.

clue: This red-rock desert town is famous for spiritual 'energy vortexes' and a chapel built into a butte.
fact: It is an International Dark Sky Community with strict lighting rules.

clue: The Emerald Buddha sits inside a royal palace complex on the Chao Phraya River in this capital.
fact: The city's full ceremonial name is one of the longest place names in the world.

clue: The labyrinthine Bronze Age palace on Crete linked to the myth of King Minos and the Minotaur.
fact: Its excavator repainted parts of it in bright colors, a choice still debated.

clue: This Pacific port hosted the 2010 Winter Olympics, where Canada won hockey gold on Sidney Crosby's overtime goal.
fact: Its Stanley Park is larger than New York's Central Park.

clue: In 1957, federal paratroopers escorted nine Black students into a high school here.
answer: Little Rock Central High School, Arkansas
fact: President Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne.

clue: President William McKinley was shot at the Pan-American Exposition here in 1901.
fact: The expo showed off electricity from nearby hydropower.

clue: A massive sandstone monolith in the desert heart of its continent that glows red at sunset; climbing it was banned in 2019.
fact: Most of the rock is hidden underground.

clue: A planned resort built on a narrow sandbar in the 1970s, now its country's top beach destination on the Caribbean.
fact: The resort's hotel strip is shaped like a giant number 7.

clue: Albert Einstein worked as a patent clerk in this capital during 1905, his 'miracle year' of physics papers.
fact: Bears have been kept in a pit here since the 1500s as a city mascot.

clue: Lakota and Cheyenne warriors wiped out George Custer's command on a river bluff here in June 1876.
fact: It's often called "Custer's Last Stand."

clue: Civil rights marchers were beaten on the Edmund Pettus Bridge here on "Bloody Sunday," March 7, 1965.
fact: The march to Montgomery helped pass the Voting Rights Act that August.

clue: A former royal palace that became a public museum in 1793; a glass pyramid was added to its courtyard in 1989.
fact: The Mona Lisa was stolen from here in 1911 by a museum handyman.

clue: Jets bombed the presidential palace in this capital during a September 1973 coup.
fact: President Salvador Allende died inside during the attack.

clue: The first international treaty requiring rich countries to cut greenhouse gases was adopted in this city in 1997.
fact: The U.S. signed it but never ratified it.

clue: "The shot heard round the world" was fired at a wooden bridge here on April 19, 1775.
fact: Ralph Waldo Emerson coined the phrase in an 1837 hymn.

clue: The river town where a young Samuel Clemens grew up and set Tom Sawyer's adventures.
fact: He took his pen name from a riverboat depth call.

clue: A 15th-century Inca citadel on a mountain ridge that Yale lecturer Hiram Bingham brought to world attention in 1911.
fact: The Spanish conquistadors never found it.

clue: King Leonidas and his 300 Spartans held a narrow coastal pass here against the Persian army in 480 BC.
fact: The coastline has since moved, and the pass is now miles wide.

clue: A red-walled palace complex that was the last Muslim stronghold on the Iberian Peninsula, surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492.
fact: Its name means "the red one" in Arabic.

clue: The lowest point in North America, 282 feet below sea level, in a valley that hit 134°F in 1913.
fact: That 134°F reading is still the hottest air temperature ever recorded on Earth.

clue: Snowbound emigrants resorted to cannibalism near a Sierra Nevada lake in the winter of 1846–47.
fact: Only about half of the 87 members survived.

clue: A white-marble mausoleum an emperor built on the Yamuna River for his favorite wife, who died in childbirth in 1631.
fact: Shah Jahan was later imprisoned by his own son and could see it from his window.

clue: About 2,750 tons of improperly stored ammonium nitrate exploded here in August 2020.
fact: The blast was felt in Cyprus, 150 miles away.

clue: Bobby Fischer beat Boris Spassky for the world chess championship in this capital in 1972.
fact: Reagan and Gorbachev held a summit there in 1986.

clue: A June 1972 break-in at a riverside office complex led to a president's resignation.
fact: A security guard noticed tape over a door latch.

clue: Two of America's greatest rivers merge beside this small town.
fact: It was a major Union supply base in the Civil War.

clue: A flat-topped mountain overlooking a port city, often draped with a "tablecloth" of cloud.
fact: It's one of the oldest mountains on Earth.

clue: The world's largest intact volcanic caldera, a natural enclosure holding about 25,000 large animals, including rare black rhinos.
fact: The crater floor is about 100 square miles.

clue: The 1992 treaty that created the European Union and set up the euro was signed in this city.
fact: The Netherlands' southernmost city is almost surrounded by Belgium.

clue: President Kennedy was shot from the sixth floor of a book depository overlooking this plaza in November 1963.
fact: An "X" on the street marks the spot of the fatal shot.

clue: The world's longest known cave system, with more than 420 miles mapped.
fact: Enslaved guide Stephen Bishop mapped much of it in the 1830s.

clue: A 6th-century domed cathedral that became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.
fact: For nearly 1,000 years it was the largest cathedral in the world.

clue: Invading forces surrendered here in June 1982, ending a 74-day war over these islands.
fact: There are more sheep than people on the islands.

clue: Edvard Munch's 'The Scream' hangs in this Nordic capital, which also has a museum of 1,000-year-old Viking ships.
fact: Every year it sends London a Christmas tree for Trafalgar Square.
